craft_claim: Unidirectional self-disclosure alone does not produce durable intimacy; the effect depends on perceived responsiveness and reciprocity, which a text must simulate through second-person address and acknowledged reader standing.

supporting_evidence.location: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 74(5): 1238-1251, results on perceived partner responsiveness
supporting_evidence.note: Perceived partner responsiveness is a partial mediator between disclosure and intimacy; intimacy is a combination of self-disclosure and partner disclosure, not disclosure alone.

supporting_evidence.location: Sections on reciprocity of exchange and reward-cost outcomes
supporting_evidence.note: Social penetration predicts reciprocity: disclosure at a given depth invites comparable disclosure and is regulated by expected rewards and costs.

supporting_evidence.location: Psychiatry 19(3): 215-229, discussion of the one-sidedness of the para-social tie
supporting_evidence.note: Para-social closeness is structurally unilateral; the persona performs responsiveness rather than actually responding.

counterevidence.note: Audiences do experience para-social bonds as genuinely intimate despite their one-sidedness, so the reciprocity requirement is a durability constraint rather than a prohibition on unilateral address.

scope: Text-simulated reader address in essay, blog, fiction, and copy.
exceptions: Forms that deliberately exploit one-sided address (e.g., the dramatic monologue) may not need simulated responsiveness.
